title: The Dhamaal Boys Are Back, Older, Greyer, and Funnier. After Seven Years, Total Madness Returns on July 10.
excerpt: Ajay Devgn, Arshad Warsi, Riteish Deshmukh and Jaaved Jaaferi reunite for Dhamaal 4 — and the trailer plus two chart-bait songs suggest Indra Kumar is betting the franchise's no-logic charm still works in 2026.
body:
Some franchises age into prestige. The **Dhamaal** films age into pure, unbothered chaos — and that, somehow, is the point. The trailer for **Dhamaal 4** dropped this month with the energy of men who know exactly what they are and refuse to apologize for it: four overgrown idiots, one impossible scheme, and a treasure hunt that will inevitably collapse into slapstick ruin. Nobody is here for the plot. Everybody is here for the bit.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=IG-eByZdz6Y</youtube>

And the bit, fifteen years on, still lands. **Ajay Devgn**, **Arshad Warsi**, **Riteish Deshmukh** and **Jaaved Jaaferi** slide back into their roles like a comfortable old pair of chappals, joined by **Sanjay Mishra** and a fresh ensemble of **Esha Gupta**, **Sanjeeda Shaikh**, **Anjali Anand**, Upendra Limaye, Vijay Patkar and **Ravi Kishan**. There is a particular pleasure in watching this gang grey at the temples and still throw themselves down a flight of comic-timing stairs. Warsi, especially, looks like he's having the time of his life. He usually is.

> "I was born dancing for songs like this." — Anjali Anand, on the Dhamaal 4 track Chatni

Director **Indra Kumar**, the franchise's founding ringmaster, knows his audience doesn't change and doesn't want to. The promotional rollout has leaned hard into music — two tracks out already, both engineered for the algorithm. First came **Chatni**, the "chatpata" item-energy number that newcomer Anjali Anand called the song she was "born dancing" for. Then this week landed **Qeher**, fronted by **Guru Randhawa**, all hook-step swagger and TikTok-ready choreography, with Ketika Sharma in a special appearance. The strategy is transparent and, frankly, effective: get the songs trending, get the gang's faces everywhere, and let nostalgia do the rest.

It's worth remembering how far this franchise has climbed on sheer silliness. The 2007 original was a sleeper hit — roughly ₹51 crore worldwide, celebrated for its audacious no-heroine, non-stop-comedy format. *Double Dhamaal* (2011) pushed it to around ₹71 crore. Then *Total Dhamaal* (2019) detonated: with Ajay Devgn, Anil Kapoor and Madhuri Dixit aboard, it pulled in roughly ₹232 crore globally and turned a goofy comedy series into a genuine box-office franchise. Seven years is a long gap, though, and the comedy landscape has shifted hard toward OTT and stand-up. The question hanging over *Dhamaal 4* is whether the big-screen, brain-off family comedy still pulls families into halls — or whether that audience now watches **India's Got Latent** on their phones.

The summer timing is aggressive. *Dhamaal 4* rolls into theatres on **July 10**, slotting into a packed Bollywood corridor that already saw *Cocktail 2* open strong and has *Welcome to the Jungle* — another legacy-comedy ensemble — landing June 26. That's two massive multi-star comedies inside a fortnight, a genuine test of whether the diaspora's appetite for big silly Hindi entertainers has limits. My take: *Dhamaal 4* is the safer bet of the two. The Welcome films can be exhausting; the Dhamaal gang has chemistry that money can't manufacture.

Produced by Ajay Devgn's Devgn Films alongside Bhushan Kumar's T-Series, Maruti International and Panorama Studios, the film arrives with serious commercial muscle behind it. For NRI audiences, a Dhamaal release is reliable comfort food — expect a wide North American, UK, Gulf and Australia theatrical rollout the same weekend, because these films travel; the diaspora has always shown up for no-stakes laughter on a Friday night abroad. A streaming home will follow within a couple of months, almost certainly on one of the major platforms that T-Series typically partners with.

There is something almost defiant about a fourth Dhamaal in 2026. It isn't chasing awards. It isn't reinventing anything. It's a franchise that figured out its formula two decades ago and has the nerve to keep serving it, loudly, to a country that keeps showing up. Whether 2026 audiences still want their comedy this broad and this big is the ₹200-crore question. But if the answer is yes, the Dhamaal boys will be the ones laughing all the way to the bank — and probably tripping over a banana peel on the way in.
